Paragraph:
Translation: Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat—and, by so doing, you shall never incur sin.

Purport (Excerpt): Lord Krsna now directly says that Arjuna should fight for the sake of fighting because He desires the battle... He who acts for his own sense gratification, either in goodness or in passion, is subject to the reaction... But he who has completely surrendered himself in the activities of Krsna consciousness is no longer obliged to anyone.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna is heavily attached to the dualities of the material world—fearing the distress of killing and doubting the happiness of victory, leading to a fear of sinful reaction (karma).
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna introduces the core principle of Karma-yoga: equanimity. He instructs Arjuna to act purely out of duty, completely detached from the dualities of happiness/distress, loss/gain, or victory/defeat. This detachment insulates him from sin.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna is given the precise formula for acting in the world without accumulating karmic baggage or psychological distress.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Equanimity: Mental calmness and evenness of temper, especially in difficult situations
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Detachment from Outcomes: Focusing on the process rather than the result
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Emotional Regulation: Managing extreme emotional swings caused by perceived wins or losses

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Karma-phala-tyaga (Renunciation of the fruits of action)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: This verse is the seed of Karma-yoga. Sin (karma) is generated when actions are motivated by material attachment (desire for gain/happiness). If an action is performed purely as an offering to the Supreme, without any personal agenda or attachment to the dualities of the outcome, the actor remains completely untainted by sin.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This is a profound lesson in emotional regulation. When we tie our psychological well-being to external outcomes (victory/defeat), we are on an emotional rollercoaster. Krishna teaches 'process over outcome.' By detaching from the uncontrollable results and focusing solely on doing the right thing in the present moment, we achieve mental equilibrium and avoid the 'sin' of psychological burnout.
